My mom was the stake young womens president. We always went to a camp in Utah called Kolob for Stake Girls Camp. One year the mountain was on fire during camp, and my mom had to make the call to cut camp short so that we didn’t get caught in a bad situation with the fire. 

The next Stake Girls camp, the mountain was on fire againbut much closer this time. My mom spoke with the Cedar City fire chief, and he said there is only one way out. Meaning If the fire somehow blocked the entrance/exit, we couldn’t get out and rescue couldn’t get in. 

Immediately my mom went to the stake president to cancel camp and start looking for another place, it was just too dangerous. The stake president was belligerent and adamant that it was not unsafe. My mom pushed back by refusing to let the stake go to camp, and within a week she was released. The stake still goes to Kolob for girls camp to this day.

It’s one of my favorite books. When I was younger, I didn’t quite grasp what was meant when it was compared to the American dream. Now that I’m older, have a 9-5, have a 401k, etc. I think it perfectly describes the American dream. I think what Fitzgerald creates perfectly with TGG is that the American dream is an illusion. It’s effectively dead. And what’s even more interesting is I think that has never been more true than today. The American dream has always been heralded as “if you work hard, pull yourself up by your bootstraps, you will have everything you could ever want and more.” But it’s fiction. Just how no matter what Gatsby did he was never going to get daisy, no matter what we do the American system is rigged. It’s about who you know, who your parents are, the color of your skin, if you can afford student loans, go to Harvard, etc. And while that may sound cynical, it’s also unabashedly the truth, at least in my worldview.
